title: On the Expressive Power of Permutation-Equivariant Weight-Space Networks
claim: Prior expressivity results are partial; we unify the equivalence of existing architectures and prove they are universal across all approximation settings.
layout: 3 columns, left-to-right; fan-out of thick arrows from one hub
description: A three-part diagram of the theory landscape. The left black-bordered box stacks five light-blue boxes for permutation-equivariant networks: DWS, NG-GNN, GMN, NFN and NFT, each with a citation. Bidirectional blue arrows between neighbors show new equivalence results. One red arrow between GMN and NFN marks a previous one-way result. In the center, a gray 'Feed-forward simulation' box receives red arrows from DWS and GMN (prior results) and has a blue arrow into the right panel. Four thick blue arrows labeled 'Universal' fan out from GMN to four right-hand boxes. Two are green (function-space functionals and operators) and two are brown (permutation-invariant functionals and permutation-equivariant operators). Each has math notation such as F→R^n. A legend at the top explains blue as new and red as previous. The eye goes to the thick blue fan.
caption: Expressivity landscape for permutation-equivariant weight-space networks on MLPs (blue arrows: new contributions; red arrows: previous results). $\WS$ and $\gF$ denote weight-space and function-space, respectively. Left: Equivalence of permutation-equivariant networks. Center: Assuming general position, all weight-space networks are universal across all approximation settings, strengthening prior feed-forward simulation results for DWS and GMN. Right: Approximation settings in weight space.
abstract: Weight-space learning studies neural architectures that operate directly on the parameters of other neural networks. Motivated by the growing availability of pretrained models, recent work has demonstrated the effectiveness of weight-space networks across a wide range of tasks. SOTA weight-space networks rely on permutation-equivariant designs to improve generalization. However, this may negatively affect expressive power, warranting theoretical investigation. Importantly, unlike other structured domains, weight-space learning targets maps operating on both weight and function spaces, making expressivity analysis particularly subtle. While a few prior works provide partial expressivity results, a comprehensive characterization is still missing. In this work, we address this gap by developing a systematic theory for expressivity of weight-space networks. We first prove that all prominent permutation-equivariant networks are equivalent in expressive power. We then establish universality in both weight- and function-space settings under mild, natural assumptions on the input weights, and characterize the edge-case regimes where universality no longer holds. Guided by our theoretical results, we show that slight modifications to existing weight-space models yield a 34% improvement over prior SOTA, demonstrating the practical relevance of our framework.
